claims.text: In that file, step 1 states the customer-care department reported about ten calls a day asking to cancel an undelivered order, and that the product owner — the person who did step 1 in this example — rewrote it as one sentence that does not say how to build it.

In that file, step 2 records that only an order with status `new` can be cancelled while an order already `paid` goes through the refunds department, and that the decision was written down because it narrows the scope a lot.
In that file, step 3 describes two people working on separate branches, each merging the newest code from the main branch into their own every day.

In that file, step 4 states the acceptance conditions were written before the code, and that the tester re-ran exactly those plus one case nobody had thought of: cancelling the same order twice in a row.
In that file, step 5 states the feature went to the real environment at the start of a week rather than on a Friday afternoon.

In that file, step 6 reports the calls fell to two a day after one week, that the team found a cancelled order still sending a notification saying it is on its way, and that this defect goes back to step 1.

That file's closing section states the six steps always happen even when nobody names them, that methods differ only in the size of one loop, and that a small loop does not produce less documentation but makes being wrong early cheaper.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: docs/team/lifecycle-example.md lines 34-39, section 'Điều đáng chú ý'

claims.text: The repository's own note states that these six steps always happen even when nobody names them; the lesson repeats that framing as the repository's, not as a standard, and uses it because the example file is organised that way.
The six steps form a loop rather than a line, because what is learned while the system runs becomes the need that starts the next trip.

When the whole system is sent around the six steps once, a decision made in the design step waits until release to meet a real user; when one small feature is sent around, it reaches release in weeks instead.
The argument for small trips is a shorter distance between a decision and the evidence that it was wrong, not less thinking or fewer written decisions.

Because the conditions were agreed before the code was written, the tester re-runs somebody else's agreement instead of deciding what correct means; the same step also finds cases the agreement missed.

Step 3 is the junior's own work; the file gives step 4 to a tester, and on many teams you also run those agreed conditions against your own code before handing it over, which makes step 4 shared rather than somebody else's (sections 5, 7, 9).

Teams often call a waterfall the shape in which each of the six steps is done once, for the whole system, before the next step starts. The lesson defines the shape by its behaviour first and offers the name as what teams commonly say, not as a standard's term.

Working in small trips is commonly called agile. The lesson gives the name only so that the quoted belief about agile can be answered, and makes no claim about any particular framework that carries the name.

The example file's trip is one small feature — a cancel button for customers — taken once around all six steps, and for that one feature the file records the need, the scope decision and the acceptance conditions.
